--- title: "Implementation Details" engine: tex execute: freeze: auto --- *Implementing the solver is easy until you have to do it yourself* ## Mesh Generation The current library was written to showcase the use of differentiable solvers. Differentiable solver refers to the differentiation of the solution (thickness, pressure or velocity) with respect to the inputs (geometry - vertices of the mesh, initial conditions, and model parameters). This framework therefore allows comparision between some of the best open-source or commercial solvers such as OpenFoam and Ansys. The current framework is limited to **OpenFoam Finite Area meshes** only. OpenFoam's Finite Area meshes has an added benefit: All the surfaces in the mesh are planar. This allows for some optimizations as expensive routines to handle non-planar or curved surfaces are avoided. It also allows for having a simple structure for the solver. The solver solves the depth averaged Savage-Hutter model assuming mild surfaces. For sharp curvatures additional steps need to be taken for the discontinuities introduced. $$ \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(h\bar{u}) = 0 $$ $$ \frac{\partial h\bar{u}}{\partial t} + \xi\nabla\cdot(h\bar{u}\bar{u}) = -\frac1\rho\tau_b + h\textbf{g}_s - \frac\alpha\rho\nabla_s(hp_b) $$ $$ \xi\nabla_n\cdot(h\bar{u}\bar{u}) = h\textbf{g}_n - \frac\alpha\rho\nabla_n(hp_b) - \frac1\rho(\textbf{n}_bp_b) $$
The depth averaged Savage Hutter model for mild surfaces
## Parsing the Mesh OpenFoam writes the mesh to text files which can be read through to get the mesh structure for the solver. This is handled in four steps. - Parse the "points" file to get the vertices of the mesh - Parse the "faces" file to get the face (edges/connectivity) of the mesh - Parse the "faceLabels" file to get the finite area mesh - Reordering points computed in step 1 to retain only the points on the surface File parsing can be done using simple conditionals or using Julia's built-in RegEx (regular expression) support. > **_NOTE:_** Since regular expressions based search can be expensive, it is used only where is required. Here's an example "points" file that the library's parser expects: Notice the structure. After the header, there is a number denoting the number of vertices "points" in the mesh. Following which is a parenthesis and the coordinates of the points. After generating several meshes using OpenFoam, this structure is observed in all of the generated files. This can be easily utilized to get the vertices of the mesh.
Implementation Explanation of this code can be found [here](here) ```julia function parsePoints(location::String; threads=true, stats=false)::Vector{Vector{FLOAT_TYPE}} t_start = Base.time() # Read file f_point_cloud = Base.open(location, "r") s_points_cloud = Base.split(read(f_point_cloud, String), '\n') Base.close(f_point_cloud) # [Advice on Stack] Only use Regex if you have to! total_points = Base.parse(Int, s_points_cloud[20]) s_points_cloud = s_points_cloud[22:22+total_points-1] # Process the string stats && println("Reading point cloud...") if stats pbar_points = ProgressBar(total=length(s_points_cloud)) end mesh_points = Vector{Vector{FLOAT_TYPE}}(undef, length(s_points_cloud)) # Preallocating for speed @maybe_threads Threads.nthreads == 1 || !threads for i in eachindex(s_points_cloud) s = split(strip(s_points_cloud[i], ('(', ')'))) mesh_points[i] = [parse(Float64, s[1]),parse(Float64, s[2]), parse(Float64, s[3])] if stats update(pbar_points) end end stats && println("Parsing points took: ", Base.time() - t_start, " seconds") # Status Update return mesh_points end ```
I won't bother you with the implementation details. The faces and faceLabels are also parsed in a similar manner. Let's move on to processing of the mesh. ## Mesh pre-processing Once the vertices of the mesh cells and the edge information is computed, its time for computing useful geometrical information about the mesh. The following data structure is used to store mesh cells. ```julia struct Cell{ center_coords center_idx vertices vertices_idx local_coords transform edge_centers edge_lengths face_normal area neighbours vel h pb } ``` This structure allows for storing geometrical data for later use and is also used as a temporary storage for intermediatary values. Following is a brief description of the fields representing geometrical data. ### Face Centers `center_coords` A center of a regular polygon can be described simply as a point which is equidistant from all vertices of the polygon. For a planar surface, a center of a regular polygon is the arithmetic mean of all its vertices. Simply put, $$\vec{center} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \vec{vertices}}{N}$$
Implementation in source code ```julia # Returns the arithmetic mean of all vertices [Face Center] function computeCenter(vertices::Vector{Vector{T}})::eltype(vertices) where T<:Union{Real, Dual} return sum(vertices) ./ length(vertices) end ``` That's quite clean. All the functions in the library are written to handle both floating point and dual numbers for normal calculations and to support automatic differentiation Time Complexity: $O(V)$ where $V$ are the number of vertices in the face.
The field `center_idx` is the index of the face in the mesh ### Surface Normals `face_normal` Computing the surface normals is easy when the surface is planar. A plane has the property that the surface normal is perpendicular to any vector in the plane. Simply put, if $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are two non-parallel vectors in the plane then the surface normal is, $$ \vec{n} = \frac{\vec{A} \times \vec{B}}{\lvert\vec{A} \times \vec{B}\rvert} $$
Implementation in source code ```julia function computeNormals(vertices::Vector{Vector{T}})::Vector{Vector{T}} where {T<:Union{Real,Dual}} l = length(vertices) if l < 2 throw("computeNormals expected atleast 2 vertices, got $l") end idx1 = 1 idx2 = idx1 % l + 1 idx3 = idx2 % l + 1 edge1 = normalize(vertices[idx2] - vertices[idx1]) edge2 = normalize(vertices[idx3] - vertices[idx2]) surface_normal = normalized_cross(edge1, edge2) return surface_normal end ``` Any two edges of a face can be used to compute the face normal and even the local coordinate system of the face Time Complexity: $O(1)$
### Edges For a regular planar polygon, every geometrical detail can be computed using simple formulas. An edge is represented by the vector connecting two vertices of face. For a regular polygon, the edge center is simply the midpoint of these vertices $$ \text{Edge Center} = \frac{\text{Vertex}_1 + \text{Vertex}_2}{2} $$ The `edge_centers` field is an array of vectors which store the face centers of all the edges. The edge length is simply the distance between the connecting vertices $$ \text{Edge Length} = \lvert \textbf{Vertex}_2 - \textbf{Vertex}_1 \rvert $$ The field `edge_lengths` is an array of scalars which contain the lengths of all the edges. ### Area `area` The area of a regular polygon can be computed by dividing the polygon into triangles. The area of a triangle $\textbf{ABC}$ is simply $$ area(\textbf{ABC}) = \frac{\lvert \vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} \rvert}{2} $$ Adding up the areas of all the triangles gives the area of the regular polygon. ### Jacobian Determinants The planar geometry of OpenFoam meshes for mild geometry have an added advantage. Both the global and local coordinate systems are Cartesian. This means that the Jacobian used for coordinate systems, expressed as, $$ J = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_2} & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_3} \\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_2} & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_3} \\ \frac{\partial f_3}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial f_3}{\partial x_2} & \frac{\partial f_3}{\partial x_3} \end{bmatrix} $$ can be solved analytically. Here $\textbf{f}$ and $\textbf{x}$ represent local and global coordinate systems. Since both the global and local coordinate systems are of the same type, they can be expressed as, $$ f_1 = J_{11} x_1 + J_{12} x_2 + J_{13} x_3 $$ $$ f_2 = J_{21} x_1 + J_{22} x_2 + J_{23} x_3 \\ $$ $$ f_3 = J_{31} x_1 + J_{32} x_2 + J_{33} x_3 $$ or more conviniently, $$ \begin{bmatrix} f_1 \\ f_2 \\ f_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} J_{11} & J_{12} & J_{13} \\ J_{21} & J_{22} & J_{23} \\ J_{31} & J_{32} & J_{33} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} $$ where $\textbf{J}$ is the jacobian. But how we calculate the jacobian? We only have the numerical values of the coordinate vectors and not their variable representations. Here's where the Cartesian nature of both coordinate systems comes handy. Because both the local and global coordinate systems are Cartesian, the local coordinate system can be represented as a 3D rotation of the global system and can be expressed simply as $$ f = R x $$ where $\textbf{R}$ is expressed as, $$ \textbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} f_1 \cdot x_1 & f_1 \cdot x_2 & f_1 \cdot x_3 \\ f_2 \cdot x_1 & f_2 \cdot x_2 & f_2 \cdot x_3 \\ f_3 \cdot x_1 & f_3 \cdot x_2 & f_3 \cdot x_3 \end{bmatrix} $$ is the direction cosine matrix (DCM). Since the DCM's are orthogonal, their determinant is $1$. This means that the Jacobian of the coordinate transformation also has the determinant $1$. This enables us to ignore the transformation determinants when transforming integrals. ### Neighbours `neighbours` Computing neighbours of a cell is an expensive operation. The library computes the neighbours using the following algorithm: - Compute the faces each point belong to - Intersect vertices connected by an edge to get the neighbour This algorithm is not efficient! In fact, the complexity of this algorithm is $O(PE)$ where $P$ and $E$ are the total number of vertices and edges respectively. Since, $P = O(E)$, the algorithm approximately has a complexity $O(E^2)$. Even though it is not the most efficient algorithm, it is quite simple to implement and easily parallelizable. ### Local Coordinate System `local_coords` This field represents the local coordinate system of the cell.
